reasons: The source explicitly presents a multi-step claim form in which injury/claim details come first and name, email, and phone number come in step two.

It directly contrasts this sequence with requesting personal information immediately, which it says can feel like lead capture, and explains that the need-details-first order feels like a diagnosis process and reduces burden after investment in the form.
The candidate appropriately scopes the action to consideration in a multi-step form and identifies the stated example fields without inventing a required number of need-detail fields.
The source expressly observes that the claim-test page is not selling the solicitor firm or discussing how great it is; it is focused solely on getting the visitor to do the test.
The candidate confines the recommendation to a CTA page like that claim-test example, rather than claiming this is a universal rule for all pages.
The source calls the kitchen CTA wording plain English and common sense, and says that it removes the possible fears discussed in that example.
The action is appropriately qualified to addressing identified possible fears, rather than claiming that every CTA can eliminate every conceivable fear.
No unsupported readability score, vocabulary requirement, or universal conversion claim is added.
The source supports the specific kitchen-design example: an address is requested only if the visitor wants a free home survey, and the speaker emphasizes that the visitor is not forced to provide it.

However, the candidate turns that single example into a general rule for all optional information requests. The source does not establish that conditional phrasing is the appropriate treatment for every optional field or context.
Revise the action to retain the example-specific scope, or frame the broader application as a consideration rather than a general instruction.

The source says visitors commonly need answers before contacting a provider and lists approximate cost, response speed, reliability and who will attend, qualifications, compatibility with the boiler, and service area in the boiler-repair scenario.
It also explains why: most visitors do initial scouting to decide whether a provider is in the right ballpark and may go elsewhere if they cannot determine that.
The candidate qualifies the items as examples of questions visitors may need answered, rather than treating the boiler-specific list as mandatory for every business.

The source explains that, after injury details have been supplied, it makes sense to ask for contact details by telling the visitor that those details are needed to send the claim assessment to the right place.
The candidate preserves the relevant condition—requesting personal details after need details in a multi-step form—and does not assert that its quoted wording is mandatory outside the example.
Its dependency on c1 is consistent with the source sequence and is not circular.

omissions.description: Provide a way for a visitor who is struggling with the questionnaire to contact a person for help during completion.
omissions.quote: If you're struggling at any point during the completion of this questionnaire and you wish to speak speak to a solicister, do not hesitate to call us on that number.

source_limitations: The excerpt begins mid-sentence and ends mid-thought, including an incomplete list of fears about the Exposure Ninja offer; surrounding qualifications and the remainder of that discussion are unavailable.
The excerpt is a spoken, example-driven presentation with transcription artifacts and incomplete phrasing, so some wording is ambiguous or informal.
The source asserts effects on perceived embarrassment and conversion but provides no measurements, study design, or performance data for the examples.
